overview.heading: Read the dog before you touch the dog
overview.intro: Dogs communicate constantly through scent, vocalization, and body posture. This lesson works through one body region at a time — ears, eyes, mouth, tail — and then puts the regions back together so you can describe what a patient is telling you and act on it safely. The habit the lesson builds is simple: when you observe, you describe what you see, and you interpret only once you have the whole picture.
objectives: Name the three channels dogs use to communicate and recognise them in a live patient.
Describe ear carriage, including the alert position and why cropped ears are hard to read.
Pay attention to the three eye characteristics: stare or avoidance, pupil size, and eye opening.
Tell a defensive grin from a submissive grin, and recognise displacement behaviours.
Interpret tail carriage, including a slow methodical wag and a low or tucked tail.
Use the terms appeasement, agonistic, and displacement correctly.
State the definition of aggression and distinguish offensive, defensive, and protective aggression.
overview.connectsForward: Reading canine communication underpins every hands-on skill that follows: restraint, physical examination, sample collection, and treatment. A patient you can read is a patient you and your team can handle safely.

modules.title: How Dogs Communicate
modules.content:
Dogs are talking to us constantly — with scent, with sound, and with their bodies. This lesson teaches you to read that conversation the way the clinical team needs to read it: describe first, interpret second.

In this module you will

  • Name the three channels dogs use to communicate.
  • Separate describing what you see from interpreting what it means.
  • Recognise appeasement, agonistic, and displacement behaviours by name.

Observation checklist

The three channels dogs use

0 of 4 revealed

Reveal each channel in turn, then watch a dog in your practice and try to catch all three.

  1. 1ScentDogs communicate through scent.
  2. 2VocalisationDogs communicate through sound. A growl is one vocalisation — and a growl is not always a threat.
  3. 3Body postureDogs communicate through the position and carriage of the whole body: ears, eyes, mouth, tail, and stance.
  4. 4All three at onceThe three channels are used together, which is why the assessment answer to “dogs communicate using?” is all of the above.

All 4 cues revealed. Replay the video and try to name each one out loud before it happens.

Observation prompt

A dog in the lobby is standing still with its ears forward and its tail high. Write down what you would put in the record.

Compare with the course answer+

Record what you see, not what you think it means: “ears forward, tail held high, standing squarely, not moving.” When you observe, you describe what you see. Interpretation is a separate step and belongs to the whole picture, not one body part.

Key vocabulary

Four words used throughout this lesson

modules.title: Observing Canine Ear Carriage
modules.content:
Ears move fast and they move first. Watching ear carriage on its own is the easiest way to start building an observation habit.

In this module you will

  • Describe the alert ear position and the head change that goes with it.
  • Explain why cropped ears are difficult to interpret.

Observation checklist

Ear carriage cues

0 of 4 revealed

Reveal one cue at a time, then re-watch the video and pause each time you see it.

  1. 1Ears pulled forwardIn the alert position the ears are pulled forward.
  2. 2Skin wrinkling on the headPulling the ears forward causes the skin on the head to wrinkle. The wrinkle is your confirmation that the ears really are forward.
  3. 3Ears held backEar carriage changes with the dog’s state, so note the position you actually see rather than assuming a fixed “normal”.
  4. 4Cropped earsDogs with cropped ears are difficult to interpret because they are not capable of much movement. Read the rest of the body instead.

All 4 cues revealed. Replay the video and try to name each one out loud before it happens.

Observation prompt

The video shows a dog whose ears go forward. What else changes on the head?

Compare with the course answer+

The skin on the head wrinkles. That is the assessment answer to “in the ______ position, the ears are pulled forward, causing the skin on the head to wrinkle” — the alert position.

modules.title: Observing Eyes and Gaze
modules.content:
Eyes carry a lot of information in a very small area. Three things are worth looking at every time.

In this module you will

  • List the three eye characteristics to pay attention to.
  • Recognise darting, scanning eyes and scrunched eyes.

Observation checklist

Eye and gaze cues

0 of 5 revealed

These are the characteristics the assessment asks you to pay attention to. Reveal them one at a time.

  1. 1Direct stare or avoidance of eye contactThe first characteristic to pay attention to is whether the dog stares directly at you or avoids eye contact.
  2. 2Pupil sizeThe second characteristic to pay attention to is pupil size.
  3. 3How open the eyes areThe third characteristic to pay attention to is how open the eyes are.
  4. 4Darting, scanning eyesEyes that dart around and constantly scan show both anxiety and fear.
  5. 5Scrunched eyesScrunched eyes are a characteristic of threatening dogs.

All 5 cues revealed. Replay the video and try to name each one out loud before it happens.

Observation prompt

A dog will not settle and its eyes keep sweeping around the room. What are you seeing?

Compare with the course answer+

Darting, constantly scanning eyes show anxiety and fear — both, not one or the other. Describe it as “eyes darting, scanning the room” and let the rest of the body confirm the picture.

modules.title: Observing the Canine Mouth
modules.content:
The mouth is where several very different messages look superficially similar. A grin is not always a grin, and a growl is not always a threat.

In this module you will

  • Separate a defensive grin from a submissive grin.
  • Recognise a vertically raised lip and what it signals.
  • Identify panting and displacement behaviours involving the mouth.

Observation checklist

Mouth and muzzle cues

0 of 7 revealed

Reveal each cue, then re-watch the video and pause on every mouth change you can find.

  1. 1A vertically raised lipA vertically raised lip is considered a threatening posture.
  2. 2Submissive grin — the eyesSubmissive grinning dogs have more closed eyes.
  3. 3Submissive grin — the lipsSubmissive grinning dogs may lick their lips.
  4. 4Defensive grin — the eyesDefensive grinning dogs keep their eyes wide open.
  5. 5PantingDogs may pant when they are anxious or stressed.
  6. 6Yawning, licking, groomingThese can be displacement behaviours.
  7. 7GrowlingA growl is not always a threat.

All 7 cues revealed. Replay the video and try to name each one out loud before it happens.

Observation prompt

Two dogs both pull their lips back. One has wide open eyes, the other has narrowed eyes and keeps licking. What is the difference?

Compare with the course answer+

The wide open eyes point to a defensive grin. The more closed eyes and the lip licking point to a submissive grin. All three of those signs — closed eyes, lip licking, wide open eyes — are how the course tells the two apart.

modules.title: Canine Tail Carriage
modules.content:
A wagging tail is the single most misread signal in a veterinary lobby. Speed and height matter more than movement.

In this module you will

  • Explain what a slow, methodical tail wag signals.
  • Explain what a low or tucked tail signals.

Observation checklist

Tail carriage cues

0 of 3 revealed

Two tail positions are named directly in this course. Reveal them and commit them to memory.

  1. 1A slow, methodical wagA slow, methodical tail wag is a threatening posture — not a friendly one.
  2. 2A tail held low or tuckedWhen a tail is held low on the body or tucked, this is a defensive posture.
  3. 3Describe before you interpretRecord the height and the speed of the tail. “Tail low, tucked under” is a description; “defensive” is the interpretation that follows.

All 3 cues revealed. Replay the video and try to name each one out loud before it happens.

Observation prompt

A dog approaches you with a slow, deliberate wag. Is it safe to reach for the collar?

Compare with the course answer+

No — a slow, methodical tail wag is a threatening posture. Slow down, read ears, eyes, mouth, and stance, and let the whole picture decide your next move.
modules.completionHeading: Reveal both tail positions, then select Continue.

modules.title: Canine Behavioral Interpretations
modules.content:
Individual cues only mean something once you put them together. This module names the postures and behaviour groups the course expects you to use.

In this module you will

  • Describe the alert posture.
  • Use the terms appeasement, agonistic, and displacement correctly.
  • Keep description and interpretation separate.

Observation checklist

Putting the cues together

0 of 7 revealed

Each item below is a term or posture named directly in this course. Reveal them in order.

  1. 1Alert postureA dog that is alert stands very straight, and may lean forward.
  2. 2Alert earsIn the alert position the ears are pulled forward, causing the skin on the head to wrinkle.
  3. 3AppeasementNon-threatening behaviours are also called appeasement.
  4. 4Agonistic behavioursBehaviours shown in social situations in which the dog feels threatened or challenged.
  5. 5Displacement behavioursYawning, licking, and grooming can be displacement behaviours.
  6. 6Submissive dogs and noiseSubmissive dogs do not often bark or growl.
  7. 7Describe, then interpretWhen you observe, you describe what you see.

All 7 cues revealed. Replay the video and try to name each one out loud before it happens.

Observation prompt

Why does the course insist that you describe rather than interpret while you are observing?

Compare with the course answer+

Because the sentence the assessment uses is “when you observe, you describe what you see.” A description can be checked by someone else; an interpretation cannot. Write the posture down, then name it.

modules.title: Interpreting Aggressive Behavior
modules.content:
Aggression has a specific definition in this course, and offensive and defensive aggression behave very differently once you step away.

In this module you will

  • State the course definition of aggression.
  • Distinguish offensive from defensive aggression.
  • Recognise the situations that trigger protective aggression.

Observation checklist

Aggression cues and categories

0 of 6 revealed

Reveal each item, then say out loud whether it is a definition, a category, or a posture.

  1. 1The definitionAggression is defined as behaviours that result in harm of the opponent.
  2. 2Offensive aggressionA dog that is offensively aggressive may chase you down the street.
  3. 3Defensive aggressionA defensively aggressive dog will not chase you down the street.
  4. 4Threatening posturesA vertically raised lip, scrunched eyes, and a slow, methodical tail wag are all named as threatening.
  5. 5Defensive posturesA tail held low on the body or tucked is a defensive posture.
  6. 6Protective aggressionIt occurs when the owner shakes hands with, is hugged by, or is handed a package by someone outside the dog’s social group — all of these.

All 6 cues revealed. Replay the video and try to name each one out loud before it happens.

Observation prompt

A client is greeted with a hug in the lobby and their dog reacts. What is this called?

Compare with the course answer+

Protective aggression. The course lists three triggers — a handshake, a hug, and being handed a package by someone outside the dog’s social group — and the assessment answer is all of the above. Greet the owner from a distance and let them manage the dog first.

Safety firstIf you read a threatening or defensive posture, stop, create distance, and get help before continuing to handle the patient. Nothing in this lesson replaces your hospital’s handling and restraint protocols.

modules.title: Final Assessment
modules.content:
Final assessment. Twenty-one scored questions drawn from the seven video modules you have just completed. One question at a time, with feedback as soon as you answer.

Before you begin

How this assessment works

Select one answer per question. Feedback appears immediately, and the next question stays hidden until you select Next. You can move back to review any question you have already answered. Your score is recorded in your Hannah Learning System progress once all questions are answered, and a score of 75% or higher marks this module — and the lesson — complete. You can retake the assessment as many times as you need.

quiz.q: Dogs communicate using?
quiz.exp: Dogs use scent, vocalization, and body posture together, so all of the above is correct.

quiz.q: Non-threatening behaviors are also called ________.
quiz.exp: Appeasement is the term used for non-threatening behaviours. Agonistic behaviours are the opposite — they are shown when the dog feels threatened or challenged.

quiz.q: If a dog’s eyes are darting around and constantly scanning, the dog is showing?
opts: Both B and C are correct.
quiz.exp: Darting, constantly scanning eyes show both anxiety and fear.

quiz.q: A slow, methodical tail wag is a ________ posture.
quiz.exp: A slow, methodical wag is threatening. Movement alone does not make a tail friendly.

quiz.q: How can you tell the difference between a defensive grin and a submissive grin?
opts: Submissive grinning dogs have more closed eyes.
Submissive grinning dogs may lick their lips.
Defensive grinning dogs keep their eyes wide open.
quiz.exp: All three signs are used to tell the two apart: more closed eyes and lip licking in the submissive grin, wide open eyes in the defensive grin.

quiz.q: Yawning, licking and grooming can be ________ behaviors.
quiz.exp: Yawning, licking, and grooming can be displacement behaviours.

quiz.q: Protective aggression occurs when ________.
opts: The owner shakes hands with someone outside the dog’s social group.
The owner is hugged by someone outside the dog’s social group.
The owner is handed a package from someone outside the social group.
quiz.exp: All three situations — a handshake, a hug, and a handed package from someone outside the dog’s social group — can trigger protective aggression.

quiz.q: When you observe, you ________ what you ________.
quiz.exp: When you observe, you describe what you see. Interpretation is a separate step.

quiz.q: Dogs with ________ ears are difficult to interpret because they are not capable of much movement.
quiz.exp: Cropped ears are not capable of much movement, so they give you far less information. Read the rest of the body instead.

quiz.q: Characteristics of a dog’s eyes that you need to pay attention to are?
opts: Direct stare or avoidance of eye contact.
quiz.exp: All three — stare or avoidance, pupil size, and how open the eyes are — are the eye characteristics to pay attention to.

quiz.q: A vertically raised lip is considered a ________ posture.
quiz.exp: A vertically raised lip is a threatening posture.

quiz.q: Scrunched eyes is a characteristic of ________ dogs.
quiz.exp: Scrunched eyes are a characteristic of threatening dogs.

quiz.q: Aggression is defined as behaviors that result in ________ of the opponent.
quiz.exp: Aggression is defined as behaviours that result in harm of the opponent.

quiz.q: A dog that is ________ stands very straight, and may lean forward.
quiz.exp: An alert dog stands very straight and may lean forward.

quiz.q: A dog that is ________ aggressive may chase you down the street, but a ________ aggressive dog won’t.
quiz.exp: An offensively aggressive dog may pursue; a defensively aggressive dog will not chase you down the street.

quiz.q: When a tail is held low on the body or tucked, this is a ________ posture.
quiz.exp: A tail held low or tucked is a defensive posture.

quiz.q: ________ behaviors are those that are shown in social situations in which the dog feels threatened or challenged.
quiz.exp: Agonistic behaviours are shown in social situations in which the dog feels threatened or challenged.

quiz.q: Dogs may pant when they are anxious or stressed.
quiz.exp: True. Panting is not only about heat — dogs may pant when anxious or stressed.

quiz.q: In the ________ position, the ears are pulled forward, causing the skin on the head to wrinkle.
quiz.exp: In the alert position the ears are pulled forward and the skin on the head wrinkles.

quiz.q: A growl is always a threat.
quiz.exp: False. A growl is not always a threat — read it together with the rest of the body.

quiz.q: Submissive dogs often bark or growl.
quiz.exp: False. Barking and growling are not typical of submissive dogs.
